text: Is the number '0' a rational number? Explain why it fits the definition of a rational number, and how it is different from an irrational number like √2.
hints: Rubric (2 marks; accept any equivalent valid method or notation): 1 mark - shows 0 can be written as p/q with integers p, q and q not 0 (e.g. 0 = 0/1). 1 mark - states √2 cannot be written as p/q (its decimal never ends or repeats).

text: Show the steps to find exactly three rational numbers between 2 and 3. Write down the simple formula or method you used to space them out.
hints: Rubric (2 marks; accept any equivalent valid method or notation): 1 mark - a valid method (common denominator, averaging, or similar). 1 mark - three correct rational numbers strictly between 2 and 3.

text: Without doing long division, explain why 7/8 will result in a terminating decimal, while 1/3 results in a non-terminating repeating decimal. What does the denominator tell you?
hints: Rubric (4 marks; accept any equivalent valid method or notation): 1 mark - 8 = 2 x 2 x 2. 1 mark - a denominator with only 2s and/or 5s as prime factors can be made a power of 10, so the decimal terminates. 1 mark - 3 is not 2 or 5, so 1/3 can never have a power-of-10 denominator and repeats. 1 mark - states the rule that the prime factors of the denominator decide.

text: A student measured a piece of wood as 0.666... meters long. Convert this repeating decimal into a fraction (p/q form) so the carpenter can mark it accurately on a ruler.
hints: Rubric (3 marks; exact conversion; accept any equivalent valid method, the variable x or this notation is not required): 1 mark - sets up x = 0.666... and 10x = 6.666... (or equivalent). 1 mark - subtracts to get 9x = 6 (or equivalent). 1 mark - solves and simplifies x = 6/9 = 2/3. A rounded value (e.g. 0.67 = 67/100) changes the number and earns 0. If the final step is missing, say: 'Your setup and subtraction are correct. Finish by dividing by 9 and simplifying: x = 6/9 = 2/3.'
